title: Assistive listening devices for improving auditory processing and school performance of children with auditory processing disorders either affecting or not affecting understanding speech in noise
summary:
Children can have problems processing and understanding what they hear in the brain, even though their ears function normally. Such disorders are called auditory processing disorders (APD). They can be treated, among other things, by speech therapy or by a remote microphone hearing system (RMHS). Currently, children in Germany only receive a system if they have a specific form of APD, namely if they have difficulty understanding speech in noisy environments. However, research suggests that children with other auditory processing and perceptual problems may also benefit from such a system. Attention, learning, classroom behavior and cooperation, school success, self-esteem, and personal development can all be enhanced by the use of such devices. Even short-term use can lead to long-term improvements in the brain's processing of auditory signals. We, the study team, expect that even small improvements in teachers' understanding in a noisy classroom through a RMHS may be critical to these children's success in school. 
Thus, the study is designed to answer the following questions: do children with APD but no difficulty understanding speech in noise benefit from wireless acoustic transmission systems? If so, how large is this benefit compared to children with APD and difficulty understanding speech in background noise? And how large is the benefit from a RMHS compared to children who do not receive such a system but receive standard speech therapy? How do auditory processing and school performance improve for all three groups?
For our study, 72 school-age children with APD between the ages of 6 and 14 are recruited for the study and assigned to three groups. Group I contains only children with difficulties in understanding speech in background noise (24 children), and Group II contains only children without these difficulties (24 children). Group III contains 12 children each with and 12 children without difficulty understanding speech in background noise. The children in groups I and II will each receive a remote microphone hearing system for 12 weeks. Only Roger Focus devices from the Phonak company are used in order to keep the conditions the same for all children and to make the study results comparable. The devices are borrowed from a local hearing care professional. The children in group III will receive speech therapy for APD once a week for 12 weeks. Group assignment will be randomized. 
All children will be assessed with comprehensive auditory processing and perception tests and questionnaires at study entry, after the 12 weeks of treatment, and 6 months after completion of the 12 weeks of treatment. Before/at baseline, some tests (hearing tests, intelligence tests, language tests) will also be administered to differentiate from other conditions and to detect common comorbidities.

interventions.name: 24 children with APD and difficulties in understanding speech in noise are treated with a RMHS (devices: Roger Focus, Phonak, loaned by a hearing aids acoustician) for 12 weeks.
24 children with APD but with other difficulties than understanding speech in noise will be fitted with RMHS for 12 weeks.

12 children with and 12 children without difficulties in understanding speech in noise in the context of an APD receive 12 weeks of a single 12-hour logopaedic APD standard therapy (one hour per week).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Participants will be enrolled in the study if.
(1) peripheral hearing loss has been ruled out by pure tone audiometry with air conduction and bone conduction thresholds at 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8 kHz (8 kHz air conduction only),
(2) a cognitive deficit has been ruled out by a nonverbal intelligence test using the Wechsler Nonverbal Scale of Ability (WNV) or the Raven's Progressive Matrices (RPM), and/or the CFT 1-R (Culture Fair Intelligence Test - Resivion),
(3) AVSD has been diagnosed by standard phoniatric-audiological and psychological testing with a test battery that includes the following tests:
a.	Speech audiometry in quiet and in noise (Oldenburg Sentence Test, OLSA or Oldenburg Children's Sentence Test, OLKISA in noise and Göttingen Children's Speech Intelligibility Test or Freiburg Test for Monosyllables in quiet).
b.	Dichotic hearing test according to Uttenweiler or Feldmann, depending on age 
c.	Mottier test (measures auditory memory, auditory sequencing and identification and differentiation of phonemes by means of chains of meaningless syllables)
d.	Repetition of Numbers subtest from the Battery for Assessment in Children - Memory and Learning Skills Test for 6- to 16-year-olds (BASIC-MLT).
e.	Verbal Learning and Memory Test (VLMT)
f.	Sentence repetition, rhyming, vowel substitution, consonant substitution, and consonant elision subtests from the Potsdam-Illinois Test of Psycholinguistic Abilities (P-ITPA).
g.	Subtests Completing words (auditory completion), Connecting sounds (auditory synthesis) from the Psycholinguistic Developmental Test (PET). 
h.	Subtests on discrimination of linguistic stimuli (place of articulation, intonation of consonants) and on just perceptible differences of non-linguistic stimuli (tone duration, frequency, sinusoidal amplitude modulation) from the Bochum Screening for Auditory and Linguistic Discrimination (BASD)
i.	Auditory discrimination subtest from the BVN/NPS neuropsychological screening test battery,
(4) parents or legal guardians and - if applicable - children have given their written consent to participate in the study.
Exclusion criteria:
Unstable medical conditions or conditions that would place the individual or the examiner at risk for injury, lack of cooperation, or lack of consent of the subject or the parents, teachers or the legal guardian.
